1.0: When Israel was brought into captivity, and Jerusalem left deserted, the prophet Jeremias sat down there and wept, with this mournful lamentation following. And as he spoke, ever he sighed and moaned in the bitterness of his heart.
1.1: Alone she dwells, the city erewhile so populous; a widow now, once a queen among the nations; tributary now, that once had provinces at her command.
1.2: Be sure she weeps; there in the darkness her cheeks are wet with tears; of all that courted her, none left to console her, all those lovers grown weary of her, and turned into enemies.
1.3: Cruel the suffering and the bondage of Juda’s exile; that she must needs dwell among the heathen! Nor respite can she find; close at her heels the pursuit, and peril on either hand.
1.4: Desolate, the streets of Sion; no flocking, now, to the assembly; the gateways lie deserted. Sighs priest, and the maidens go in mourning, so bitter the grief that hangs over all.
1.5: Exultant, now, her invaders; with her enemies nothing goes amiss. For her many sins, the Lord has brought doom on her, and all her children have gone into exile, driven before the oppressor.
1.6: Fled is her beauty, the Sion that was once so fair; her chieftains have yielded their ground before the pursuer, strengthless as rams that can find no pasture.
1.7: Grievous the memories she holds, of the hour when all her ancient glories passed from her, when her people fell defenceless before the invader, unresisting before an enemy that derided them.
1.8: Heinously Jerusalem sinned; what wonder if she became an outlaw? How they fell to despising her when they saw her shame, that once flattered her! Deeply she sighed, and turned away her head.
1.9: Ill might skirts of her robe the defilement conceal; alas, so reckless of her doom, alas, fallen so low, with none to comfort her! Mark it well, Lord; see how humbled I, how exultant my adversary!
1.10: Jealous hands were laid on all she treasured; so it was that she must see Gentiles profane her sanctuary, Gentiles, by thy ordinance from the assembly debarred.
1.11: Kindred was none but went sighing for lack of bread, offered its precious heirlooms for food to revive men’s hearts. Mark it well, Lord, and see my pride abased!
1.12: Look well, you that pass by, and say if there was ever grief like this grief of mine; never a grape on the vineyard left to glean, when the Lord’s threat of vengeance is fulfilled.
1.13: Must fire from heaven waste my whole being, ere I can learn my lesson? Must he catch me in a net, to drag me back from my course? Desolate he leaves me, to pine away all the day long with grief.
1.14: No respite it gives me, the yoke of guilt I bear, by his hand fastened down upon my neck; see, I faint under it! The Lord has given me up a prisoner to duress there is no escaping.
1.15: Of all I had, the Lord has taken away the noblest; lost to me, all the flower of my chivalry, under his strict audit; Sion, poor maid, here was a wine-press well trodden down!
1.16: Pray you, should I not weep? Fountains these eyes are, that needs must flow; comforter is none at hand, that should revive my spirits. Lost to me, all those sons of mine, outmatched by their enemy.
1.17: Quest for consolation is vain, let her plead where she will; neighbours of Jacob, so the Lord decrees, are Jacob’s enemies, and all around they shrink from her, as from a thing unclean.
1.18: Right the Lord has in his quarrel; I have set his commands at defiance. O world, take warning; see what pangs I suffer, all my folk gone into exile, both man and maid.
1.19: So false the friends that were once my suitors! And now the city lacks priests and elders both, that went begging their bread, to revive the heart in them.
1.20: Take note, Lord, of my anguish, how my bosom burns, and my heart melts within me, in bitter ruth. And all the while, sword threatens without, and death not less cruel within.
1.21: Uncomforted my sorrow, but not unheard; my enemies hear it, and rejoice that my miseries are of thy contriving. Ah, but when thy promise comes true, they shall feel my pangs!
1.22: Vintager who didst leave my boughs so bare, for my much offending, mark well their cruelty, and strip these too in their turn; here be sighs a many, and a sad heart to claim it.

2.1: Alas, what mantle of cloud is this, the divine anger has thrown over unhappy Sion? The pride of Israel cast down from heaven to earth; the ground where the Lord’s feet once rested, now, in his anger, forgotten?
2.2: Blessed abodes of Jacob, by the Lord’s unsparing vengeance engulfed; towers that kept Juda inviolable hurled to the ground in ruin; kingdom and throne dragged in the dust!
2.3: Crushed lay all the defences of Israel, under his displeasure; failed us, at the enemy’s onset, the protection of his right hand; Jacob must be hedged about, as by flames of a consuming fire.
2.4: Deadly his bent bow, steady the play of his right hand assailing us; all that was fairest in poor Sion’s dwelling-place needs must perish, under the fiery rain of his vengeance.
2.5: Enemies he counts us, and has engulfed the whole of Israel in ruin; gone the palaces, gone the strongholds; Alas, poor Sion! weeps man, weeps maid, with cowed spirits.
2.6: Fallen, as it had been some garden shed, his own tabernacle; his own trysting-place with men he would pull down! Feast-day and sabbath should be forgotten in Sion; for king and priest, only anger and scorn.
2.7: Grown weary of his altar, from his own sanctuary turning away in abhorrence, the Lord has given up yonder embattled towers to the enemy; their cries ring through the temple like shout of holiday.
2.8: Heedfully the Lord went about his work, to strip the inviolable city of her walls; exact his measuring-line, busy his hand with the task of overthrow, till wall and rampart should lament their common ruin.
2.9: Idly the gates of her sag towards earth, bars riven and rent; king and chieftain are far away, exiled among the heathen; tradition is dead, nor any prophet learns, in vision, the Lord’s will.
2.10: Jerusalem’s aged folk sit there in the dust, dumb with sorrow; dust scattered over their heads, and sackcloth their garb; never a maid shall you see but has her head bowed down to earth.
2.11: Keen anguish for the overthrow of an unhappy race, that dims eye with tears, that stirs my being to its depths, as my heart goes out in boundless compassion! Child and babe lie fainting in the streets.
2.12: Listen, how they ask where all the bread and wine is gone to! Wound they have none, yet there in the open streets you shall see them faint away, sighing out their lives on their mothers’ bosoms.
2.13: Might I but confront thee with such another as thyself! What queen so unhappy as Jerusalem, what maid as Sion desolate? How shall I comfort thee? Sea-deep is thy ruin, and past all cure.
2.14: Never a true vision or a wise thy prophets have for thee, never shew thee where thy guilt rests, and urge thee to repentance; lies and lures are all the burden of their revealing.
2.15: Openly the passers-by deride thee, poor maid; clap hands, and hiss, and wag their heads at thee; So much, they cry, for the city that was once the nonpareil of beauty, pride of the whole earth!
2.16: Pale envy mops and mows at thee; how they hiss and gnash their teeth! Now to prey on her carrion! What fortune, that we should have lived to see this day, so long looked for in vain!
2.17: Quit is the Lord of his oath taken in times past; all his purpose is fulfilled; for thee, ruin relentless, for thy bitter enemy, triumph and high achievement.
2.18: Round those inviolable defences, cry they upon the Lord in good earnest. Day and night, Sion, let thy tears stream down; never rest thou, never let that eye weary of its task.
2.19: Sleepless in the night-watches raise thy song; flow thy heart’s prayer unceasingly; lift ever thy hands in supplication for infant lives; yonder, at the street corner, they are dying of famine.
2.20: Think well, Lord, is there any other people of whom thou hast taken such toll? Shall woman eat her own child, so tiny, hands can still clasp it? In the Lord’s sanctuary, priest and prophet be slain?
2.21: Untended they lie on the bare earth, the young and the aged; maid and warrior slain by the sword! This day of thy vengeance was to be all massacre, thou wouldst kill unsparingly.
2.22: Vengeance this day all around me; what mustering of thy terrors, as for a solemn assembly! Escape is none, nor any remnant left; of all I fondled and fostered, the enemy has taken full toll.

3.1: Ah, what straits have I not known, under the avenging rod!
3.2: Asked I for light, into deeper shadow the Lord’s guidance led me;
3.3: Always upon me, none other, falls endlessly the blow.
3.4: Broken this frame, under the wrinkled skin, the sunk flesh.
3.5: Bitterness of despair fills my prospect, walled in on every side;
3.6: Buried in darkness, and, like the dead, interminably.
3.7: Closely he fences me in, beyond hope of rescue; loads me with fetters.
3.8: Cry out for mercy as I will, prayer of mine wins no audience;
3.9: Climb these smooth walls I may not; every way of escape he has undone.
3.10: Deep ambushed he lies, as lurking bear or lion from the covert;
3.11: Drawn aside from my path, I fall a lonely prey to his ravening.
3.12: Dread archer, of me he makes a target for all his arrows;
3.13: Each shaft of his quiver at my vitals taught to strike home!
3.14: Evermore for me the taunts of my neighbours, their songs of derision.
3.15: Entertainment of bitter herbs he gives me, and of wormwood my fill,
3.16: Files all my teeth with hard gravel-stones, bids me feed on ashes.
3.17: Far away is my old contentment, happier days forgotten;
3.18: Farewell, my hopes of long continuance, my patient trust in the Lord!
3.19: Guilt and suffering, gall and wormwood, keep all this well in memory.
3.20: God knows it shall be remembered, and with sinking of the heart;
3.21: Gage there can be none other of remaining confidence.
3.22: His be the thanks if we are not extinguished; his mercies never weary;
3.23: Hope comes with each dawn; art thou not faithful, Lord, to thy promise?
3.24: Heart whispers, The Lord is my portion; I will trust him yet.
3.25: In him be thy trust, for him thy heart’s longing, gracious thou shalt find him;
3.26: If deliverance thou wouldst have from the Lord, in silence await it.
3.27: It is well thou shouldst learn to bear the yoke, now in thy youth,
3.28: Just burden, in solitude and silence justly borne.
3.29: Joy may yet be thine, for mouth that kisses the dust,
3.30: Jeering of the multitude, and cheek buffeted in scorn, bravely endured.
3.31: Know for certain, the Lord has not finally abandoned thee;
3.32: Kind welcome the outcast shall have, from one so rich in kindness.
3.33: Kin of Adam he will not crush or cast away wantonly;
3.34: Let there be oppression of the poor under duress,
3.35: Law’s right denied, such as the most High grants to all men,
3.36: Lying perversion of justice, then he cannot overlook it.
3.37: Man may foretell; only the Lord brings his word to pass;
3.38: Mingled good and evil proceed both from the will of the most High;
3.39: Mortal is none may repine; let each his own sins remember.
3.40: Narrowly our path scan we, and to the Lord return;
3.41: Never hand or heart but must point heavenward this day!
3.42: Nothing but defiant transgression on our part; and shouldst thou relent?
3.43: Over our heads thy angry vengeance lowered; smiting, thou wouldst not spare.
3.44: Oh, barrier of cloud, our prayers had no strength to pierce!
3.45: Offscouring and refuse of mankind thou hast made us,
3.46: Put to shame by the mocking grimaces of our enemies.
3.47: Prophets we had, but their word was peril and pitfall, and ruin at the last.
3.48: Poor Sion, for thy calamity these cheeks are furrowed with tears;
3.49: Quell if thou wouldst the restless fever of my weeping,
3.50: Quickly, Lord, look down from heaven and pay heed to us,
3.51: Quite forspent, eye and soul, with grief Jerusalem’s daughters bear.
3.52: Relentless as hawk in air they pursued me, enemies unprovoked,
3.53: Reft me of life itself, sealed with a stone my prison door.
3.54: Round my head the waters closed, and I had given myself up for lost,
3.55: Save for one hope; to thee, Lord, I cried from the pit’s depth,
3.56: Sure of thy audience; wouldst thou turn a deaf ear to sighs of complaint?
3.57: Summoned, thou didst come to my side, whispering, Do not be afraid.
3.58: Thine, Lord, to take my part; thine to rescue me from death;
3.59: The malice of my enemies to discover, my wrongs to redress.
3.60: Thrust away from thy sight, the grudge they bear me, the ill they purpose,
3.61: Unheard by thee their taunts, their whispered plottings?
3.62: Uttered aloud or in secret, their malice assails me from morn till night;
3.63: Up in arms, or met in secret conclave, ever against me they raise the battle-song.
3.64: Visit them with the punishment their ill deeds have earned;
3.65: Veiled be those blind hearts with fresh blindness of thy own making;
3.66: Vanish from the earth their whole brood, ere thy vengeance leaves off pursuing them!

4.1: All dim, now, and discoloured, the gold that once shone so fair! Heaped up at every street-corner lie hallowed stones.
4.2: Bright they shone once in all their renown, the men of Sion, and now what are they? Little regarded as common earthenware, of the potter’s fashioning.
4.3: Cub of jackal is fed at its dam’s breast; and has my people grown unnatural towards its own children, like some ostrich in the desert?
4.4: Dry throat and parching tongue for babe at the breast; children asking for bread, and never a crust to share with them!
4.5: Ever they fared daintily, that now lie starved in the streets; ever went richly arrayed, and now their fingers clutch at the dung-hill.
4.6: Faithless Juda! Heavier punishment she must needs undergo than guilty Sodom, that perished all in a moment, and never a blow struck.
4.7: Gone, the fair bloom of princely cheeks, snowy-pure, cream-white, red as tinted ivory, and all sapphire-clear;
4.8: Here is no recognizing them, out in the streets, coal-black, skin clinging to bones, dry as wood!
4.9: It were better to have fallen at the sword’s point than yield thus to the stab of hunger, wasted away through famine.
4.10: Juda brought low, and mother-love forgotten; that women should eat their own children, cooked with their own hands!
4.11: Kindled at last is the Lord’s anger; rains down from heaven the storm of his vengeance, lighting a flame that burns Sion to the ground.
4.12: Little dreamed they, king and common folk the world over, that any assault of the foe should storm Jerusalem gates;
4.13: Malice and lawlessness it was of priest and prophet, whereby innocent men came to their deaths, that brought such punishment.
4.14: Now, as they walk blindly through the streets, they are defiled with blood; no help for it, gather their skirts about them as they may;
4.15: Out of my way! cries one to another; Back, pollution, do not touch me! The very Gentiles protest in alarm, Here is no place for them!
4.16: Protection the Lord gives them no longer, they are dispersed under his frown; the priesthood no honour claims, old age no pity.
4.17: Quenched is the hope our eyes strained for, while hope was left us; looking for help so eagerly to a nation that had none to give!
4.18: Refuge for us in the treacherous highways is none; we are near the end; all is over, this is the end;
4.19: Swifter than flight of eagles the pursuit; even on the mountains they give chase, even in the desert take us by surprise.
4.20: Through our fault he who is breath of life to us, our anointed king, is led away captive; under his shadow we hoped our race should thrive.
4.21: Until thy turn comes, shout on, Edom, triumph on, land of Hus; the same cup thou too shalt drink, and be drunken, and stripped bare.
4.22: Vengeful audit-day! Sion’s account closed, recovered her fortunes; Edom called to account, discovered her guilt!

5.1: Bethink thee, Lord, of our ill case; see where we lie humiliated, and seeing take pity!
5.2: New tenants our lands have, our homes foreign masters;
5.3: orphaned sons of widowed mothers were not more defenceless.
5.4: Ours to buy the very water we drink, pay a price for every stick of fire-wood;
5.5: led hither and thither under the yoke, with no respite given,
5.6: we must make our peace with men of Egypt or Assyria, for a belly-full of bread.
5.7: So must we bear the guilt of our fathers, that sinned and are gone!
5.8: Slaves for our masters now, and none to ransom us;
5.9: bread won out in the desert, and at peril of our lives from the sword’s point!
5.10: What wonder if our skins are burnt dry as an oven, seared by long famine?
5.11: Never a woman in Sion, never a maid in all Juda’s cities, but has met with dishonour;
5.12: merciless hands hurry our princes to the gallows; reverence is none for grey hairs.
5.13: Toiling at the mill, the flower of our youth, or staggering under loads of wood;
5.14: never an old man left to sit at the gate, or a young man to wake the echoes of the harp;
5.15: gone, all our mirth, all our music drowned in sadness.
5.16: Alas, we are sinners; the wreath has faded from our brows;
5.17: there are sad hearts everywhere, and dim eyes.
5.18: What, does not the hill of Sion lie desolate, ravaged by the foxes?
5.19: Lord, thou abidest ever; age after age thy throne endures;
5.20: and wilt thou still be forgetful of us, through the long years leave us forsaken?
5.21: Bring us back to thee, Lord, and let us find our home; bring back to us the days of our youth;
5.22: wouldst thou altogether abandon us, shall thy indignation know no measure?
